modules.name: Adler
modules.header:
Adler-32, the checksum the zlib format ends with.
Two running sums modulo 65521, the largest prime below 2^16: one of the bytes and one of those sums. It is weaker
than a CRC on short messages, and kept for the formats that require it rather than recommended for new ones.

modules.name: Crc
modules.header:
CRC-32, the checksum that answers "did these bytes arrive intact?" — and its Castagnoli variant, which answers it
better and is what modern formats and hardware use.
A cyclic redundancy check is division: treat the message as a polynomial over GF(2), divide by a fixed generator,
and keep the remainder. What that buys over a sum is a guarantee rather than a hope — a 32-bit CRC detects every
burst error up to 32 bits long, every single-bit and double-bit error, and every error of odd weight, which no
general-purpose hash promises about anything.
Both forms here are the reflected, table-driven ones every implementation uses: bits enter least significant end
first, the state starts at all ones, and the answer is the state complemented. Those three conventions are not
arbitrary — the initial ones make leading zero bytes change the answer, and the final complement makes trailing
ones do the same, so a message padded at either end is not mistaken for the message itself.
The two differ only in the generator. CRC-32 uses the IEEE 802.3 polynomial that gzip, PNG and zip all use.
CRC-32C uses Castagnoli's, which detects more of the double-bit errors that matter at the lengths storage systems
care about, and which x86-64 and AArch64 both implement in hardware — iSCSI, ext4, Btrfs and SCTP all chose it.
This implementation is the table, not the instruction: correct everywhere, and about a byte per cycle.
A CRC is a checksum, not a hash and emphatically not a digest. It detects accident, never intent: given any
message and any target value, producing a message with that CRC is arithmetic a beginner can do. It implements
`Hasher` because feeding it bytes has the same shape, not because it is a substitute for one.
https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc3385

modules.name: Fnv
modules.header:
FNV-1a, the hash to reach for when the input is short and the code must be obvious.
Fowler-Noll-Vo is a byte at a time: exclusive-or the byte into the accumulator, then multiply by a prime chosen so
that every input byte reaches every output bit. There is no block buffer, no padding and no finalization, which is
why an implementation fits on a page and why hashing four bytes costs four multiplies rather than a round of
mixing that assumed sixteen.
That simplicity is also its limit. FNV-1a has no key, its structure is public, and finding two inputs that collide
is a small computation — so it must not key a table whose contents an adversary chooses. `SipHash` is the answer
there. For a compile-time constant, a short identifier, or a checksum over data nobody is attacking, FNV-1a is
smaller and faster than anything that would replace it.
Both widths are the standard ones: the 32-bit and 64-bit parameters from the FNV specification, unmodified. A hash
computed here will match any other correct implementation, which is what makes it worth naming an algorithm rather
than promising only "some hash".
https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-eastlake-fnv-21

modules.name: Hasher
modules.header:
What every hash in this package implements, and the pieces every caller of one needs.
A hash here is built the same way regardless of algorithm: make one, write bytes into it in order, and ask for the
answer. That shape is what lets a value be hashed without first being turned into a contiguous buffer — a struct
writes each of its fields in turn, and a collection writes each of its elements, with nothing copied anywhere.
Take a hasher by generic bound rather than as an owning interface value: `func Digest<H: Hasher>(hasher: &var H)`
borrows the caller's own hasher and resolves at instantiation. The interface exists to be the bound.
None of these are cryptographic. They are fast, they are named, and they are documented — but an adversary who
gets to choose the input can find collisions in any of them except `SipHash`, and even `SipHash` promises only
that it is hard without the key. Anything that must resist an adversary belongs in `Rux/Crypto`.

modules.name: SipHash
modules.header:
SipHash-2-4, the hash that keeps a table fast when someone is trying to make it slow.
Every other hash in this package has a fixed, public structure, so anyone can compute inputs that collide. Feed a
few thousand of those to a hash table and every one lands in the same bucket: lookups that should be constant
become linear, and a service that was doing fine falls over on traffic that looks perfectly ordinary. That attack
is what SipHash exists to stop.
It stops it by being keyed. Without the key, finding two inputs that collide is as hard as breaking the function,
and the key is a secret the program picks at startup — from `Rux/Entropy` — and never publishes. An attacker who
cannot guess it cannot aim. The keying is real cryptographic keying rather than a seed mixed in for luck, which is
the difference between this and `XxHash64`.
The price is speed: two rounds per eight bytes of input and four more at the end, against xxHash64's one round per
eight bytes across four independent lanes. For a hash table's short keys the difference is small and worth paying.
For hashing a large file it is not, and `XxHash64` is the better answer there.
This is not a general-purpose message authentication code either, despite the resemblance. Sixty-four bits is
enough to make collisions unfindable at hash-table scale and not enough to authenticate a message; `Rux/Crypto`
has HMAC for that.
https://www.aumasson.jp/siphash/siphash.pdf

modules.name: XxHash
modules.header:
xxHash64, the hash to reach for when there is a lot of data and the answer must be ready before the next cache
miss.
Where FNV-1a takes one byte at a time, this takes thirty-two: four independent 64-bit accumulators, each mixing
its own eight bytes with a multiply and a rotate, so a wide machine has four chains to run at once instead of one
dependency chain to wait on. The accumulators are folded together at the end, the length is mixed in, and the tail
is finished eight, four and one byte at a time.
The mixing is arithmetic rather than table lookup, which is what keeps it fast on data that does not fit in cache:
there is no table to evict. The final avalanche — shift, multiply, shift, multiply, shift — is what makes a
one-bit change in the input change about half the output bits, which the round function alone does not give.
A seed is part of the algorithm here, not an afterthought: two runs with different seeds produce unrelated hashes
of the same input, which is enough to stop accidental collisions from following data between two tables. It is not
enough to stop a deliberate one — xxHash is not keyed in the cryptographic sense, and an adversary who learns the
seed can find collisions as easily as without it. `SipHash` is the answer where that matters.
The result matches the reference implementation exactly, for every input length and every seed.
https://github.com/Cyan4973/xxHash/blob/dev/doc/xxhash_spec.md

to the caller's state without copying it.
An implementation must give the same answer for the same sequence of bytes, whatever the writes were split into:
writing eight bytes at once and writing them one at a time must agree. It must not read anything but the bytes it
is given — no address, no counter, no clock.

A hasher keyed with `low` and `high`, with nothing written into it yet.
Both halves are read by value. The key must be unpredictable to whoever supplies the input — draw it from
`Rux/Entropy` at startup and keep it. A fixed key compiled into a program is a published key, and a published
key is no key at all.
Cannot fail. Runs in constant time and allocates nothing.

params.name: low
params.markdown: the key's first eight bytes as a word

params.name: high
params.markdown: the key's second eight bytes as a word

doc.returns: a hasher keyed with those two words

doc.summary: A hasher keyed with the sixteen bytes at `key`, least significant byte of each half first.
doc.markdown:
A hasher keyed with the sixteen bytes at `key`, least significant byte of each half first.
`key` is borrowed and read. This is the byte order the specification and every published test vector use, so
it is what to reach for when checking against one; `WithKey` is what to reach for when the key came from
`Rux/Entropy` as two words.
Cannot fail. Runs in constant time and allocates nothing.
Safety: `key` must be readable for sixteen bytes.

params.name: key
params.markdown: sixteen key bytes, read as two little-endian words

doc.returns: a hasher keyed with them

doc.summary: Puts the hasher back to where it started, keeping its key.
doc.markdown:
Puts the hasher back to where it started, keeping its key.
`self` is borrowed mutably. Everything written so far is forgotten; the key is not.
Cannot fail. Runs in constant time and allocates nothing.

members.name: Write
members.signature: pub func Write(&var self, bytes: *byte, length: uint)

doc.summary: Adds `length` bytes at `bytes` to the hash.
doc.markdown:
Adds `length` bytes at `bytes` to the hash.
`bytes` is borrowed and read; `length` is read by value. A zero length changes nothing and is the one case in
which `bytes` may be null. Input that does not fill an eight-byte word is held until the rest arrives, so any
division of the same byte stream into writes gives the same answer.
Runs in time proportional to `length` and allocates nothing.
`bytes` must be readable for `length` bytes.

params.name: length
params.markdown: how many bytes; zero absorbs nothing

doc.summary: The hash of everything written so far.
doc.markdown:
The hash of everything written so far.
`self` is borrowed. Nothing is consumed: the finishing rounds run on a copy of the state, so asking twice
gives the same answer and writing more continues from where the writes left off.
Cannot fail. Runs in constant time and allocates nothing.
doc.returns: the hash of everything written since the last reset

doc.summary: The eight bytes at `bytes` as a 64-bit word, least significant byte first.
doc.markdown:
The eight bytes at `bytes` as a 64-bit word, least significant byte first.
`bytes` is borrowed and read. Assembled a byte at a time, so the answer is the same at any address on any
machine: SipHash is defined on a little-endian byte stream rather than on the machine's own order.
Cannot fail. Runs in constant time and allocates nothing.
Safety: `bytes` must be readable for eight bytes.
doc.returns: them as a little-endian word

doc.summary: The SipHash-2-4 of `length` bytes at `bytes`, keyed with `low` and `high`.
doc.markdown:
The SipHash-2-4 of `length` bytes at `bytes`, keyed with `low` and `high`.
`bytes` is borrowed and read; the rest are read by value. A zero length gives the hash of the empty input under
that key, and is the one case in which `bytes` may be null.
Cannot fail. Runs in time proportional to `length` and allocates nothing.
`bytes` must be readable for `length` bytes.

params.name: low
params.markdown: the key's first eight bytes as a word

params.name: high
params.markdown: the key's second eight bytes as a word

doc.returns: their keyed hash

doc.markdown: The first xxHash64 prime, which every round multiplies by.

doc.summary: The second xxHash64 prime, which scales each input lane before it is rotated in.
doc.markdown: The second xxHash64 prime, which scales each input lane before it is rotated in.

doc.summary: The third xxHash64 prime, used in the four-byte tail step and the avalanche.
doc.markdown: The third xxHash64 prime, used in the four-byte tail step and the avalanche.

doc.summary: The fourth xxHash64 prime, added after each merge and after each eight-byte tail step.
doc.markdown: The fourth xxHash64 prime, added after each merge and after each eight-byte tail step.

doc.summary: The fifth xxHash64 prime, which seeds an input too short to fill a block and mixes each trailing byte.
doc.markdown: The fifth xxHash64 prime, which seeds an input too short to fill a block and mixes each trailing byte.

doc.summary: How many bytes one xxHash64 round consumes: four lanes of eight.
doc.markdown:
How many bytes one xxHash64 round consumes: four lanes of eight.
An input shorter than this never touches the accumulators at all, which is why the short and long paths give
different-looking code for the same algorithm.

doc.summary: The eight bytes at `bytes` as a 64-bit value, least significant byte first.
doc.markdown:
The eight bytes at `bytes` as a 64-bit value, least significant byte first.
`bytes` is borrowed and read. Assembled a byte at a time rather than read as a word, so the answer is the same at
any address on any machine — xxHash is defined on a little-endian byte stream, not on whatever the machine
happens to hold.
Cannot fail. Runs in constant time and allocates nothing.
Safety: `bytes` must be readable for eight bytes.
doc.returns: them as a little-endian word

doc.summary: The four bytes at `bytes` as a 32-bit value, least significant byte first.
doc.markdown:
The four bytes at `bytes` as a 32-bit value, least significant byte first.
`bytes` is borrowed and read. Assembled a byte at a time, for the same reason as `ReadLittleEndian64`.
Cannot fail. Runs in constant time and allocates nothing.
Safety: `bytes` must be readable for four bytes.
doc.returns: them as a little-endian half word

items.name: XxRound
items.signature: pub func XxRound(accumulator: uint64, lane: uint64) -> uint64

doc.summary: One accumulator round: mix `lane` into `accumulator`.
doc.markdown:
One accumulator round: mix `lane` into `accumulator`.
Both are read by value and the new accumulator is returned. This is the whole of xxHash64's inner loop — scale
the input, add, rotate, scale again — and it is what the four lanes each run independently.
Cannot fail. Runs in constant time and allocates nothing.

params.name: lane
params.markdown: the input word to fold into it

doc.returns: the lane's new value

items.name: XxMerge
items.signature: pub func XxMerge(hash: uint64, accumulator: uint64) -> uint64

doc.summary: Folds one finished accumulator into the running hash.
doc.markdown:
Folds one finished accumulator into the running hash.
Both are read by value and the new hash is returned. The accumulator is passed through a round from zero first,
so a lane that happened to end at a convenient value does not stay convenient.
Cannot fail. Runs in constant time and allocates nothing.

params.name: accumulator
params.markdown: the lane to merge into it

doc.returns: the merged hash

doc.summary: The final mixing step, which spreads every input bit across the whole result.
doc.markdown:
The final mixing step, which spreads every input bit across the whole result.
`hash` is read by value and the finished hash is returned. Without this a one-bit change in the input moves only
the bits the round function reached; with it, about half of them move.
Cannot fail. Runs in constant time and allocates nothing.
doc.returns: it with every input bit spread across the output

doc.summary: xxHash64 over a stream of bytes, in as many writes as the caller has.
doc.markdown:
xxHash64 over a stream of bytes, in as many writes as the caller has.
Copy, but large: thirty-two bytes of pending input plus its accumulators. Borrow one by reference unless a
snapshot of the hash so far is what is wanted.

fields.doc: Input that has arrived but does not yet fill a block.

doc.summary: A hasher with nothing written into it yet, using `seed`.
doc.markdown:
A hasher with nothing written into it yet, using `seed`.
`seed` is read by value. Two hashers with different seeds give unrelated answers for the same input, which is
enough to keep accidental collisions from following data from one table to another. It is not enough to stop
a deliberate collision: an adversary who knows the seed is no worse off than one hashing without it.
Cannot fail. Runs in constant time and allocates nothing.
doc.returns: a hasher seeded with it

doc.summary: Puts the hasher back to where it started, keeping its seed.
doc.markdown:
Puts the hasher back to where it started, keeping its seed.
`self` is borrowed mutably. Everything written so far is forgotten; the seed is not.
Cannot fail. Runs in constant time and allocates nothing.

members.signature: pub func Write(&var self, bytes: *byte, length: uint)

doc.summary: Adds `length` bytes at `bytes` to the hash.
doc.markdown:
Adds `length` bytes at `bytes` to the hash.
`bytes` is borrowed and read; `length` is read by value. A zero length changes nothing and is the one case in
which `bytes` may be null. Input that does not fill a block is held until the rest of it arrives, so any
division of the same byte stream into writes gives the same answer.
Runs in time proportional to `length` and allocates nothing.
`bytes` must be readable for `length` bytes.

params.name: length
params.markdown: how many bytes; zero absorbs nothing

doc.summary: The hash of everything written so far.
doc.markdown:
The hash of everything written so far.
`self` is borrowed. Nothing is consumed: asking twice gives the same answer, and writing more continues from
where the writes left off rather than starting over.
Cannot fail. Runs in time proportional to what is held pending, which is under one block. Allocates nothing.
doc.returns: the hash of everything written since the last reset

The xxHash64 of `length` bytes at `bytes`, using `seed`.
`bytes` is borrowed and read; `length` and `seed` are read by value. A zero length gives the hash of the empty

Cannot fail. Runs in time proportional to `length` and allocates nothing.

doc.returns: their seeded hash

doc.markdown:
The xxHash64 of `length` bytes at `bytes`, seeded with zero.
`bytes` is borrowed and read; `length` is read by value. This is what every published xxHash64 test vector means
by "the hash of" an input.
Cannot fail. Runs in time proportional to `length` and allocates nothing.
Safety: `bytes` must be readable for `length` bytes.
